headline: Highest risk is medium: Airflow’s broad egress can feed Opik’s REST-facing observability path, creating default-config data leakage and cascading trust issues; no direct prompt-injection bridge is evidenced.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: No shared communication channel, clipboard, or filesystem bridge is documented between airflow and opik. Airflow is non-runnable here and only exposes API calls; opik exposes REST API calls. Without a documented ingestion path from one agent’s outputs into the other’s instruction parser, prompt injection is not plausible from the profiles alone.
conditions: IF a shared filesystem, clipboard, or message queue is added between airflow and opik, reassess injection risk.
IF either agent begins parsing the other’s raw text as instructions, the pathway becomes plausible.
mitigations: Keep the agents on separate workspaces.
Disable any copy-paste or shared-queue bridge.
Add provenance tags to any exchanged text.
Review parsers for instruction-like content handling.

B_data_leakage.rationale: Airflow has broad network egress, and opik exposes a REST API surface; that combination can move workflow context off-box in default deployments. Neither profile lists secrets or sensitive classes, so this is not high, but the pair still creates a realistic leakage path through transmitted context and logs.
conditions: IF airflow tasks send file contents or logs to opik’s REST API, leakage risk is active.
IF either agent is configured to ingest shared workspace artifacts, sensitive material can flow between them.
mitigations: Restrict airflow egress to allowlisted endpoints.
Redact logs before sending them to opik.
Separate workspaces for each agent.
Disable automatic artifact upload.
Audit outbound requests for payload contents.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Both agents have broad network egress, but neither profile shows filesystem write, git, database, or OAuth write scopes. That leaves only limited overlap on outbound connectivity, so direct capability conflict is small and not enough for medium severity.
conditions: IF both agents are granted write access to the same mutable resource, conflict risk increases.
IF a shared orchestrator adds locking-free writes, reassess severity upward.
mitigations: Assign distinct network allowlists.
Avoid shared mutable resources.
Use per-agent service accounts.
Add simple lock files for any shared state.

D_cascading_error.rationale: Airflow can generate operational outputs that opik may ingest through its REST API, so A’s output can become B’s input in default integrations. The profiles do not prove blind trust or downstream action-taking, so high is not justified, but the trust chain is still plausible without a verification step.
conditions: IF opik consumes airflow-produced summaries or metrics without validation, cascading error is active.
IF airflow outputs are used as authoritative inputs to downstream evaluation, errors can propagate.
mitigations: Insert a validation step before opik ingestion.
Require schema checks on airflow outputs.
Flag low-confidence fields for manual review.
Keep raw and derived outputs separate.
Log source provenance with each record.

E_compliance.rationale: Neither profile lists regulated data classes, residency constraints, certifications, or retention policies, so no concrete compliance mismatch is evidenced. Airflow and opik are both open/source-available tooling profiles here, but that alone does not establish a residency or certification conflict.
conditions: IF regulated data classes are introduced into either agent’s workflow, compliance must be re-evaluated.
IF residency or retention policies differ for the same data class, reassess severity.
mitigations: Document data classes before deployment.
Map retention settings for both agents.
Keep regulated data out of the pair until reviewed.
Record residency requirements in the runbook.
